channel.description: Noticias de ciencia de todas las fuentes configuradas.

item.title: China's Shenzhou-24 space flight takes off with Pakistani national as first foreign astronaut
item.description: China is promoting the Tiangong space station as a hub for international cooperation while the NASA-led International Space Station faces possible retirement by 2030. Publicado también por: The Hindu - International. Fuente: The Jerusalem Post - International.
item.dc:creator: BY REUTERS

item.title: Consistent friendship groups linked to longer lives in dolphin populations
item.description: Researchers analysed 40 years of data on a population of around 400 wild Indo-Pacific bottlenose dolphins living in the eastern gulf of Shark Bay. Fuente: ABC News Australia.
item.dc:creator: Stephen Clarke

item.title: Ultrathin 'rainbow' sails could power spacecraft and shade the Earth
item.description: For years, whimsically minded space enthusiasts have been dreaming of sailing across the vastness of the void on beams of sunlight. Photons, the massless particles that make up those beams of sunlight, still carry momentum and can therefore impart a gentle push when they bounce off a surface. This force is the concept behind "solar sailing," which has been having a bit of a moment in the last decade as several proof-of-concept flights have shown it is indeed feasible. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: How alfalfa forms root nodules without rhizobia
item.description: A research team led by professor Feng Jian at the Institute of Genetics and Developmental Biology (IGDB) of the Chinese Academy of Sciences has uncovered a cytokinin–NODULE INCEPTION (NIN) regulatory module associated with spontaneous root nodule formation in alfalfa (Medicago sativa). Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: New chemical route delivers first synthesis of plant compound with cough-suppressing potential
item.description: Neotuberostemonine, a complex plant-derived alkaloid with promising antitussive activity, has remained a challenging target for chemical synthesis for nearly 30 years. Researchers have now achieved its first total synthesis, alongside the synthesis of neostenine and the putative structure of tuberostemonine L. The findings also reveal how the nearly planar geometry of nitrogen atoms contributes to the oxidative instability of these alkaloids, offering new insights and synthetic strategies for natural-product chemistry and future drug discovery. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Middle-aged women in England least likely to successfully quit smoking, study finds
item.description: Of nearly 8,000 women who tried to stop, only 18% of those aged 45 to 60 managed to give up Middle-aged women in England are the least likely to successfully give up smoking, according to research . Smoking is the leading cause of preventable death and illness in the UK. While overall smoking rates in England have declined in recent decades, rates in some regions have increased. About 6.75 million people smoke in England, of whom around 14% are women aged 45-60. Continue reading... Fuente: The Guardian - World.
item.dc:creator: Anna Bawden

item.title: Quantum ingenuity can sidestep limits of conventional chips—while using commercially accessible components
item.description: For decades, computers have steadily grown faster and more powerful. Avik Dutt, an assistant professor of mechanical engineering at the University of Maryland, envisions another dramatic leap forward—one propelled by the quantum properties of light. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Laser light reveals where electrons accumulate in atomically thin semiconductor stacks
item.description: Stacking semiconductors—the chips that power phones, computers and so much more—enables quicker signal movement with less energy, but how does the process actually work? Turns out shining a literal light on the semiconducting materials can help elucidate how the electrons move in the stack, according to a multi-institutional team in Japan. The approach could help inform the development of more efficient, low-power electronics, the researchers said. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Underwater robots reveal first salp species known to live exclusively in deep sea
item.description: Salps are barrel-shaped gelatinous animals that play an important role in ocean ecosystems. More than 20 years ago, researchers observed an unfamiliar salp in the deep waters of Monterey Bay. Using specimens and data collected by MBARI's advanced underwater robots, Larry Madin, deputy director emeritus at the Woods Hole Oceanographic Institution and an MBARI adjunct, recently published a detailed description of the glass salp (Vitreosalpa gemini) in the journal Marine Biodiversity. This striking species is the first salp known to live exclusively in the deep sea. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: China’s Shenzhou-24 spacecraft lifts off with first foreign astronaut on board
item.description: China’s latest crewed space mission, Shenzhou-24, lifted off on Wednesday morning, taking three astronauts – including the first foreign crew member – to the Tiangong space station. In a sign of the space programme’s increasing diversity, for about a week, the station will be home to four astronauts from mainland China, one from Hong Kong and one from Pakistan. A Long March-2F rocket carrying the spacecraft blasted off from the Jiuquan Satellite Launch Centre in the northwestern province of... Fuente: South China Morning Post.
item.dc:creator: Ji Siqi

item.title: New workflow advances programmable chromosome editing in plants
item.description: A study published in Nature Protocols on Nov. 17 presents a detailed experimental workflow for programmable chromosome manipulation in plants. The platform was developed by a research group led by Gao Caixia at the Institute of Genetics and Developmental Biology of the Chinese Academy of Sciences. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Catalysts come alive—electron microscopy reveals the secret dynamic life of nanoparticles
item.description: University of Nottingham researchers have uncovered hidden nanoscale transformations that could help design cleaner fuels and more efficient catalysts. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: England has largest frailty gap out of 31 countries, study finds
item.description: People from lowest socioeconomic group in all countries studied had higher frailty scores than those in highest socioeconomic group England has the largest gap between higher and lower socioeconomic groups when it comes to frailty compared with 30 other countries, a major study has found. The research, led by academics at King’s College London and published in BMC Medicine, looked at levels of frailty in 71,703 people from 31 countries including England, the US, China, France, Italy, the Netherlands, Sweden, Greece, Cyprus, Latvia and Lithuania. Continue reading... Fuente: The Guardian - World.
item.dc:creator: Tobi Thomas Health and inequalities correspondent

item.title: Mitochondria rebranding: Goodbye, powerhouse of the cell. Hello, lungs of the cell?
item.description: If you remember one thing from high school biology, there's a good chance it's this: Mitochondria are the powerhouse of the cell. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Local protein supply chain keeps nerve cells' mitochondria in check
item.description: Some tracers used in hospital scans to check what is happening inside a patient's body are so short-lived they must be made on demand on site or rushed in by courier. A new study led by Angelika Harbauer's group at the Max Planck Institute for Biological Intelligence shows that nerve cells use similar strategies to deliver a protein that checks for damage in their mitochondria, the tiny structures that supply energy, balance calcium levels and perform other vital tasks. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: New nose drops restore youthful memory and fight Alzheimer’s in aging mice
item.description: A revolutionary new nasal treatment has restored youthful learning and memory performance in aging mice while preventing severe cognitive decline in mice with Alzheimer’s-like disease. Developed using technology similar to COVID-19 mRNA vaccines, the nose drops stimulate production of a brain-protecting protein that strengthens neurons and supports memory. Remarkably, the treatment preserved brain function without removing Alzheimer’s-associated plaques, suggesting a completely different way to combat cognitive decline. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: Sex in Britain has changed significantly, especially among young people
item.description: The sex lives of people in Britain have shifted markedly since 1990, and their sexual and reproductive health needs are substantial and varied, according to the fourth National Survey of Sexual Attitudes and Lifestyles (Natsal-4). The first five papers from the survey—one of the largest studies of sexual behavior in the world—are published in The Lancet. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Microplastics in nearly 8 in 10 fish sampled off Oman's Sohar coast
item.description: Researchers at Sultan Qaboos University detected microplastics in the gills or digestive tracts of 95 of 120 fish sampled off Sohar in the Sea of Oman. Published in Scientific Reports, the study provides a baseline for tracking microplastic pollution in fish along this stretch of Oman's coast. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Blind sample test reveals how BepiColombo could decode Mercury's mineral makeup
item.description: An international team of researchers, including scientists from Planetary Science Institute (PSI), has demonstrated that instruments aboard the BepiColombo spacecraft can operate together to identify the minerals that make up Mercury's surface, addressing a longstanding challenge in planetary science. The findings, published in Planetary and Space Science, come as the joint European Space Agency (ESA) and Japan Aerospace Exploration Agency (JAXA) mission entered orbit around Mercury this week. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Carbon-rich soil near old oaks does not attract more earthworms, study finds
item.description: Solitary oaks in traditional Romanian wood pastures create islands of carbon-rich soil around their trunks. However, a research team led by the Universities of Göttingen and Hildesheim found this does not mean more earthworms. In traditional wood pastures in Romania, the topsoil near the trunk held about a third more organic carbon and a quarter more nitrogen than the open grassland, yet earthworm numbers were no higher. As such trees decline across Europe, it is important to understand what they contribute to the soil. The results were published in the journal Agroforestry Systems. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Self-assembling nanocarriers show promise for delivering CRISPR to tumors and slowing growth
item.description: A self-assembling supramolecular nanocarrier protects Cas9 RNPs from degradation, enhances systemic delivery and preferential tumor accumulation, and enables pH-responsive intracellular release. Developed by researchers at the Institute of Science Tokyo, this platform achieved a 37.2% indel frequency at the luciferase target locus in HeLa-Luc tumor tissue in mice, compared with 1.5% with free RNPs, and suppressed tumor growth in separate mouse models. These findings support the further development of systemic CRISPR-based cancer therapies. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Half of NASA's aging Mars fleet knocked offline by technical issues
item.description: Perseverance is having trouble transmitting to Earth. Odyssey is rapidly burning through its waning fuel supply. Fuente: Ars Technica.
item.dc:creator: Stephen Clark

item.title: Named 'Maria,' a new species of amphibian pays tribute to the world's most popular name
item.description: Maria, the most popular female name in Brazil and around the world, was chosen for a new species of caecilian, a type of amphibian commonly known as a "blind snake," found in this South American country. The researchers chose the name Siphonops maria to raise awareness of this little-known animal, even among researchers in the field. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: The enjoy-able effect: Why fun makes us feel more skilled than we are
item.description: Picture a hobby, a game or an activity you love. Maybe it's cooking or Wordle or playing pickup basketball. For a long time, I have loved playing video games. Now ask yourself: How good are you at it? Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: NASA Hubble's new view of NGC 4394 raises the bar
item.description: A brilliant galaxy with a distinct galactic bar takes center stage in this NASA/ESA Hubble Space Telescope image. The galaxy, called NGC 4394, is in the constellation Coma Berenices (Berenice's Hair). At about 55 million light-years away, NGC 4394 is considered relatively nearby for a galaxy. It's one of more than 1,000 galaxies that make up the Virgo Cluster, which is the galaxy cluster closest to us. Publicado también por: NASA. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Quantum blueprint maps a practical path to testing unusual entanglement
item.description: Adrian Del Maestro knows how to engineer a quantum fingerprint. Rick Mukherjee has a gift for tuning atoms. Their combined expertise has taken a theory sketched out on paper and created a pathway for real experiments. The results, published in the journal Physical Review Letters, move a law-defying "mathematical oddity" ever so slightly up the technology readiness scale Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Too much to do, but too little time? 5 tips to tackle your to-do list
item.description: With the holidays approaching and the semester winding down, to-do lists are growing. Between shopping for gifts, planning gatherings, studying for finals and finishing projects, there's plenty to accomplish before the end of the year. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Flowers in Renaissance sculpture may reveal political ambitions of Florence's ruler
item.description: A new study suggests that the flowers adorning Benvenuto Cellini's sculpture Narcissus are more than decoration: they connect the development of botanical science with competition among Renaissance artists and the ambition of Florence's ruler to consolidate his status. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Why mega-constellations have a hidden space junk blind spot
item.description: We are consistently launching more and more stuff into space. As of now, space agencies track more than 30,000 objects larger than a softball, with an expected 1 million more bullet-sized pieces of debris orbiting Earth that are too small to spot from the ground. Government agencies and private commercial entities are planning to have up to 100,000 active spacecraft in orbit by the early 2030s, turning some orbital shells into crowded highways. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: A new reason for magic numbers: Scientists discover the secret behind an unusually stable molecular cluster
item.description: Why are some groups of molecules remarkably stable while others readily break apart? Researchers at Bar-Ilan University have discovered a surprising explanation for why clusters containing exactly six molecules of glycine, the simplest amino acid, are exceptionally stable—making six a "magic number." Moreover, they have uncovered the reason for this increased stability. The secret lies in a transformation that takes place when the molecules come together: they change their structure and become zwitterions, allowing them to form stronger bonds with one another. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Mindfulness training may bring out the worst in some employees
item.description: Contrary to popular belief, mindfulness training in the workplace can make some employees angrier and more likely to treat coworkers with disrespect. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Researchers reveal inner-core structural evolution of Typhoon Bavi using multisensor satellite observations
item.description: Tropical cyclones frequently undergo rapid, complex structural changes within their inner cores, such as eyewall replacement and wind-field expansion, that strongly influence typhoon intensity and coastal hazards. However, capturing these multilayered transformations continuously from the ocean surface to the upper cloud tops remains a major observational challenge. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: DNA at nuclear edges forms protective UV shield in developing roundworm embryos
item.description: Inside the cell nucleus, DNA is arranged into neighborhoods, some of which are tightly packed and mostly inactive. This so-called heterochromatin typically associates with the nuclear lamina, a meshwork lining the inside of the nuclear envelope. This arrangement helps organize the genome and regulate gene activity. But how and when it forms during embryonic development has remained unclear. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Why disaster risks are systemic and co-evolutionary
item.description: Disasters rarely happen in isolation. New research highlights the need to rethink how we assess disaster risks by recognizing how natural hazards, the people and places exposed, and their vulnerability are interconnected and change over time. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: The two ways rings are carved around a newborn star
item.description: How are planets formed in a solar system? While the question is simple, the answer is not so straightforward. Astrophysicists have long peeked into the sky, observing early stars and planets to find the answer. A common pattern observed in early stars is sequential rings of bright and dark areas emanating from the center, like grooves on a vinyl record. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: NASA+ Content Coming to Big Screen at Greenbelt, Maryland Cinema
item.description: NASA announced Monday that NASA+ content has found its first theatrical home at The Greenbelt Cinema in Greenbelt, Maryland, expanding the agency’s reach across major viewing platforms and bringing space even closer to home. “The National Aeronautics and Space Act of 1958 calls us to share our story of space exploration with the broadest possible […] Fuente: NASA.
item.dc:creator: Gerelle Q. Dodson

item.title: Teams Lock in Mission Architecture for NASA’s SR-1 Freedom
item.description: NASA completed a major review for Space Reactor-1 (SR-1) Freedom and locked in key elements of the spacecraft, which is targeted to launch in 2028 and demonstrate nuclear electric propulsion in deep space for the first time. Experts from across the agency, the U.S. Department of Energy (DOE), and industry met at NASA’s Glenn Research […] Fuente: NASA.
item.dc:creator: Heather Baeslack

item.title: A black hole the size of an atom could destroy an entire star
item.description: MIT scientists have discovered that tiny black holes left over from the Big Bang could slowly devour stars from within, eventually triggering spectacular explosions visible across galaxies. Detecting these unusual cosmic events could reveal the existence of primordial black holes and help solve the mystery of dark matter. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: Amateur Astronomer? Be a Kilonova Catcher!
item.description: Neutron stars are the ultra-dense, city-sized leftovers of dead stars. When they collide, they can release a brief flash of light called a kilonova. These immensely powerful events forge much of the universe’s gold, platinum and other heavy elements. Since a kilonova fades within days, astronomers have to find it fast, and no single observatory […] Fuente: NASA.

item.title: NASA’s Northrop Grumman CRS-25 Mission Overview
item.description: NASA’s Northrop Grumman Commercial Resupply Services 25 mission, or Northrop Grumman CRS-25, will deliver about 11,000 pounds of science and supplies to the International Space Station. The mission will be the third flight of the company’s Cygnus XL, the larger, more cargo-capable version of the company’s solar-powered spacecraft. The Cygnus XL will launch aboard a […] Fuente: NASA.
item.dc:creator: Joseph Zakrzewski

item.title: AGU Hyperwall Schedule
item.description: American Geophysical Union (AGU) 2026 Join NASA in the Exhibit Hall (Booth #525) for Hyperwall Storytelling by NASA experts. Full Hyperwall Agenda below. TUESDAY, NOVEMBER 17 10:30 AMHigh Resolution Hydrology Simulations and Agentic Super Intelligence Interfaces for Mapping Water Availability and ExtremesSujay Kumar11:00 AMScale-Resolving CFD Methods for Predicting Aircraft “Edge of the Flight Envelope” PerformanceJared […] Fuente: NASA.

item.title: Bajo esta apariencia cuqui y rechonchita, se esconde un auténtica máquina de matar. La buena noticia es que sabemos por qué
item.description: El domingo 11 de diciembre de 2016, hacia las once de la mañana, dos topillos rojos picoteaban semillas bajo un comedero de Joensuu, al este de Finlandia. Una idílica escena campestre ( a 15 grados bajo cero ). Entonces apareció un gavilán y, tras él, una urraca. Se formó la gozadera: las dos aves se enzarzaron en una pelea y, en palabras del dueño , volaron las plumas por todo el jardín. Como daño colateral, uno de los topillos cayó a la nieve; pero ninguna se lo llevó. Al topillo se lo comió el ave que menos esperábamos: un carbonero. En Xataka Investigadores de Princeton empiezan a… Fuente: Xataka.
item.dc:creator: Javier Jiménez

item.title: A unified framework for carbon dioxide removal—with an ocean view
item.description: When it comes to reducing atmospheric carbon, most roads lead to the sea. That's only natural, since the ocean is Earth's largest accessible repository for CO₂. Even without interventions to enhance its ability to capture carbon, the ocean holds about 50 times more carbon than the atmosphere and more than 20 times more carbon than plants, animals and soil combined. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Getting blood out of bone
item.description: "Jurassic Park" gave us a mosquito in amber, dinosaur DNA and a fantastic argument against opening a theme park. No mosquitoes were needed for this recent discovery, because the dinosaur fossil preserved its own bloody evidence of a land before time. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: New theoretical model allows for sustained entanglement between diamond qubits at greater separations
item.description: In a new study accepted in the journal Physical Review B, a team of physicists from the University of Delaware may have found a way to overcome limitations in maintaining the entanglement of diamond qubits. The model involves driving the qubits away from equilibrium using microwave radiation while the surrounding material is allowed to remain in equilibrium. The approach allows for both long-range and steady-state entanglement of the qubits. The paper is published on the arXiv preprint server. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Simple 'grow-and-repel' rule explains how brain immune cells organize themselves to protect nervous tissue
item.description: Imagine you need to cover a large territory with trees, ensuring no gaps are left. What is the most efficient way to plant them? This is the spatial puzzle faced by microglia, the immune cells of our brain. During development, these cells must spread across the nervous tissue to monitor and protect, yet there is no central coordinator: each cell senses only its immediate surroundings. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: New research reveals a bias in employee reference checks
item.description: When managers are asked to provide a reference for an employee, they may be doing more than describing that person's performance. They may also be promoting themselves. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Four decades of citizen science reveal widespread declines in native plant distributions in Japan
item.description: A new study led by researchers at Kyushu University has found that nearly 45% of 1,864 native plant species surveyed across Kanagawa Prefecture, Japan, were recorded in fewer locations over approximately four decades. The findings, published in Communications Biology on Sept. 15, 2026, show how long-running citizen science surveys can reveal biodiversity changes that conventional assessments focused on threatened species may miss. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Tiny tracker reveals the longest ever recorded hummingbird migration
item.description: Small though they may be, hummingbirds are no slouches when it comes to long-distance flight. These tiny birds can migrate thousands of miles across countries and continents. And now researchers have revealed the longest hummingbird migration to date—an impressive 6,526-kilometer journey (4,055 miles) from Alabama to Alaska in just 38 days. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Webb Reveals New Details in Supernova Remnant
item.description: NASA’s James Webb Space Telescope reveals the hot dust that makes up Cassiopeia A (Cas A) in this high-resolution, mid-infrared image released on Nov. 23, 2026. Remnants like these are the clouds of gas and dust that remain following the explosion of a massive star and will eventually seed a new generation of stars and […] Fuente: NASA.
item.dc:creator: HQ Web Team

item.title: Ice near Antarctica's surface could unlock climate clues millions of years old
item.description: Some of the oldest clues to Earth's climate history lie surprisingly close to Antarctica's surface. Researchers at the Vrije Universiteit Brussel (VUB) are exploring the potential of these ancient archives, with a new scientific perspective coinciding with two Antarctic field expeditions. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Water signals could guide future efforts to image supermassive black hole shadows
item.description: University of Hawaiʻi at Mānoa researchers are exploring a new way to study some of the universe's most mysterious objects: supermassive black holes. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Having fun learning with an app like Duolingo? You might be learning less than you think
item.description: Apps like Duolingo aim to make learning as enjoyable as possible. But enjoyment can also make you feel you are learning more than you actually are. This is the finding of research by Tilburg marketing researchers Robert Smith and Anna Paley. In an experiment with a language-learning app, participants who completed a more enjoyable learning task believed that they learned more than they actually did. The study is published in the Journal of Marketing Research. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Deep-sea clam discovered living inside the throat of a sea urchin
item.description: A new species of bivalve has been discovered living inside the esophagus of a deep-sea urchin in one of the most unusual partnerships known among clams. Named Vaticinaria gulicola, it was found on the abyssal seafloor of the Great Australian Bight, at depths of about 4,000 to 5,000 meters (13,100 to 16,400 feet). Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: NASA may get $2 billion boost as White House seeks to accelerate Artemis
item.description: "Without this funding, activities would be delayed." Fuente: Ars Technica.
item.dc:creator: Eric Berger

item.title: Designing and optimizing genetic circuits in biology
item.description: Although genetic circuits are important tools in synthetic biology and related fields, such as health care and sustainable manufacturing, designing them to function reliably can be challenging and often requires extensive laboratory testing and optimization. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Nigeria - Nasarawa State: Multi-Sector Needs Assessment (MSNA) 2026 data collection coverage, 3 Sep - 24 Sep 2026
item.description: Country: Nigeria Source: IMPACT Initiatives Please refer to the attached Map. Fuente: ReliefWeb - Emergencias.
item.dc:creator: IMPACT Initiatives

item.title: Four radiation belts surrounded Earth for weeks after 2024 solar superstorm
item.description: Within Earth's magnetic field, energetic particles are trapped in two doughnut-shaped regions known as the Van Allen radiation belts—usually separated by a gap where particles are especially sparse. This structure can be dramatically rearranged during solar storms, but until now, astronomers have remained largely unsure as to how this happens. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: NASA’s Titan-Bound Dragonfly Rotorcraft Gets Its Eyes
item.description: Science instruments for NASA’s Dragonfly are starting to arrive at the Johns Hopkins Applied Physics Laboratory (APL) in Laurel, Maryland, where the car-sized rotorcraft is coming together for its mission to explore Saturn’s largest moon, Titan. First to check in: DragonCam, which consists of seven cameras designed to characterize Titan’s surface at multiple scales during […] Fuente: NASA.

item.title: Offshore wind turbine hum may make phytoplankton grow faster
item.description: They are single-celled, tiny and vital to life on Earth. Phytoplankton, which drift freely in the water column, provide food and oxygen for other marine organisms, while consuming CO₂ and nutrients—much like plants on land. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Ancient cellular machinery boosts immunity against cancer
item.description: Cornell researchers have found a novel way to boost immunity against cancer: using ancient virus-derived machinery to produce tiny extracellular vesicles that carry antigen information across long distances to rally immune cells. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Q&A: How socioeconomic status is measured can obscure inequalities in health care
item.description: Socioeconomic differences in health may be greater than research suggests. In a new thesis, Balram Rai used PSA testing in the Stockholm region as an example and investigated how socioeconomic position can be measured at different levels and how measurement errors can affect inferences about inequalities in health. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Roads store microplastics before they join rain runoff to waterways
item.description: QUT researchers have developed a modeling framework to quantify microplastic inputs from urban surfaces to ecologically sensitive water environments such as Moreton Bay. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Diverse diets may reflect choice, not scarcity, among Australian hunters 45,000 years ago
item.description: A decade-long project in remote northwestern Australia suggests archaeologists should rethink a long-held assumption about the diets of humans almost 50,000 years ago. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Engineers develop simpler, scalable way to make diamond nanowires
item.description: Engineers have long known that diamond could transform modern electronics because of its exceptional hardness and superior thermal conductivity, but building with it remains challenging. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Study explores how gratitude can become a character trait
item.description: Gratitude lists can help anyone recognize the good things in their lives and feel more positive. But do they inspire people to give back? Research by BYU psychology professor Jenae Nelson suggests that becoming a grateful person takes more than counting blessings. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Six ways teens can better protect themselves from online harms
item.description: It's been nearly a year since Australia's under-16 social media ban came into effect. The restrictions were touted as a measure to protect young people from harmful design features that keep them online longer, while shielding them from risks that come with using social media. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Warmer water reshapes venom chemistry in tiny jellyfish
item.description: The tiny Irukandji jellyfish Carukia barnesi lives in the waters of northern Australia, predominantly in Queensland, with similar species in Western Australia. Irukandji stings can be lethal. These stings can cause a range of symptoms—nausea, muscle pain, vomiting and traumatic psychological effects. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Outsmarting deadly fungi: Researchers identify promising strategy against emerging fungal infections
item.description: By targeting the biological processes that determine fungal virulence, microbiologists from Stellenbosch University are suggesting a promising new strategy for combating emerging fungal infections. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: NASA Hubble’s New View of NGC 4394 Raises the Bar
item.description: The brilliant galaxy NGC 4394 with its distinct galactic bar takes center stage in this Hubble Space Telescope image Fuente: NASA.

item.title: Bull shark records reveal links between warmer waters, rainfall and activity near Queensland beaches
item.description: One of Australia's largest and longest studies of bull shark habits has identified their preferred conditions for nearshore swimming—and warmer waters in summer and autumn are top of the list. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Indigenous land management practices can deliver improved conservation outcomes, study notes
item.description: Indigenous fire management in Australia provides one of the world's best examples of how traditional methods can protect fire-prone environments, and this inclusive approach should be prioritized in modern conservation, according to research led by Charles Darwin University (CDU). Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Strategies to ensure DEI workforce safeguards in hospitality and tourism
item.description: While right-leaning governments around the world are railing against workforce diversity, equity and inclusion (DEI) measures that have been in place for over two decades, researchers note that the diversity of staff within hospitality and tourism businesses around the world—and the diverse customers they serve—requires a strong DEI framework to best serve these industries. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Beneficial fungus could offer a new way to control strawberry powdery mildew
item.description: Strawberry powdery mildew (PM), caused by the fungus Podosphaera fragariae, is a serious disease that can affect leaves, flowers, fruit and other aerial parts of strawberry plants. Infection can reduce both crop yields and fruit quality. The disease often first appears as white patches on the underside of leaves before spreading to the upper surface, making early detection challenging. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: A simple metal is hiding a strange new form of magnetism
item.description: Scientists have discovered a strange form of magnetism in an ordinary-looking metal that has no overall magnetization yet profoundly changes how electrons behave. The breakthrough offers a promising new path toward understanding exotic quantum materials and developing future electronic technologies. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: 2,200-year-old Roman shipwreck reveals an ingenious waterproofing trick
item.description: A 2,200-year-old Roman shipwreck has revealed sophisticated waterproofing techniques involving pine tar and beeswax. Microscopic pollen grains trapped in the ancient coatings are now helping scientists reconstruct where the vessel may have traveled and undergone repairs more than two millennia ago. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: Cannabis users develop psychosis years earlier, and the gap grows with age
item.description: A major analysis of 149 studies found that cannabis users develop psychosis an average of 2.5 years earlier than non-users, with the difference growing to more than six years among adults 30 and older. Researchers warn that cannabis-related psychiatric risks may accumulate over time, challenging the belief that using marijuana after adolescence is relatively safe. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: Scientists discover a new type of depression that common antidepressants struggle to treat
item.description: Researchers have discovered a new subtype of depression that may affect nearly one in four people with severe, recurrent, or persistent depression. Known as "circadian depression," it is linked to the body's internal clock and is associated with night owl tendencies, excessive sleep, persistent exhaustion, and more severe symptoms. Traditional antidepressants often work less effectively for these individuals, potentially explaining why some people struggle to find relief. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: Ancient rocks from the Moon’s far side rewrite the Solar System’s violent past
item.description: Scientists studying ancient rocks from the Moon’s far side have uncovered surprising evidence that challenges decades of thinking about the Solar System’s violent past. Instead of a single catastrophic bombardment, asteroid impacts appear to have declined gradually over billions of years, revealing new clues about Earth's early evolution and the origins of life. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: Earth's next ice age may have already begun. Global warming stopped it
item.description: Scientists have uncovered surprising evidence that Earth’s next ice age may have already begun, only to be stopped by global warming. By studying ancient plants preserved beneath the Barnes Ice Cap in the Canadian Arctic, researchers discovered that the remnants of a massive ice sheet began expanding again about 2,000 years ago, signaling the possible start of a new glacial period. But by the 1960s, rising temperatures had reversed that growth, causing the ice to shrink instead. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.description: NASA’s Voyager 1, humanity’s farthest spacecraft, is about to reach one light-day from Earth, more than 16 billion miles away; Know what it means Fuente: The Hindu - International.

item.title: Eruption Extends Iwo Jima’s Beach
item.description: A volcanic eruption just off the southeast shore of the Pacific island has reshaped the coast, but it’s unclear how long the new land will survive. Fuente: NASA.

item.title: IBM quantum computer solves problem classical computers can’t in just 15 minutes
item.description: IBM and University of Chicago researchers have demonstrated that a quantum computer can complete an extraordinarily complex calculation in just 15 minutes, beyond the practical reach of leading classical computing methods. A novel error-detection technique also allows scientists to establish confidence in the accuracy of the results, overcoming a major hurdle in quantum computing. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: America is building just 10% of the power lines it needs, experts warn
item.description: America’s power grid is falling dangerously behind as electricity demand skyrockets, fueled by data centers, electric vehicles, and industry. The U.S. is building only 10% of the new high-voltage transmission lines experts say it needs, threatening higher energy prices and greater blackout risks. Researchers argue that political obstacles and outdated regulations, rather than technological limitations, are the real problem. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: Workplace absenteeism: Why temporary disability is a right, not an expense
item.description: Temporary disability is a cornerstone of the public Social Security system. It is a right for all workers who fall ill and a social security benefit designed primarily to protect those who are sick, enabling them to receive medical treatment and recover or improve their condition while ensuring they have sufficient income during periods in which they are unable to work. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: New light-conversion tool could help speed up quantum computing
item.description: Want to break down some basics in the world of quantum research over dinner? Researchers at the Cockrell School of Engineering have you covered. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: AI has solved a host of big math problems—here's why this threatens the whole field of mathematics
item.description: For many, the year 2026 will be remembered as the one when mathematics had an identity crisis and forever changed. Frontier (cutting-edge) AI models made by OpenAI and Anthropic made stunning progress on hundreds of open problems that have baffled mathematicians for decades—and centuries in some cases. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Earth’s ancient oceans may have fooled scientists about its oxygen history
item.description: Earth’s journey from an oxygen-starved world to a planet capable of supporting complex life may have unfolded very differently than scientists once believed. A new analysis suggests that oxygen accumulated in the atmosphere in three major stages, with the oceans taking millions or even hundreds of millions of years to catch up. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: Do a violin's physical characteristics really improve with regular playing?
item.description: There is a widespread notion among violinists: A violin "opens up" as it is played, which is to say its sound gradually improves. However, an experiment conducted by a team led by a CNRS researcher has challenged this belief in a study published in Acta Acustica. After six months, the professional soloist in charge of playing the violin judged the process complete, reporting that the instrument had become easier to play and its tone had improved. Yet, no physical or acoustic measurement confirmed that this feeling resulted from such a mechanical change in the instrument itself. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Genetic mosaic helps explain diverse forms of Darwin's finches
item.description: Darwin's finches are known for their varied beaks, which help them take advantage of different food sources in the Galápagos Islands. Much previous research has focused on seed-eating ground finches, but their relatives that search for insects in forested areas have received less attention. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Recipe for one of the world's most important cancer drugs uncovered: Tobacco plants could produce the medicine
item.description: More people around the world will receive a cancer diagnosis at some point in their lives. As this trend is expected to continue, researchers have been working to crack the code of how the widely used cancer drug Taxol (paclitaxel) is naturally produced, with the aim of making its production cheaper and more efficient in the future. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Strange new materials can crawl, walk, and dig like living creatures
item.description: Scientists have developed remarkable materials that can crawl, walk, and dig using their own internal energy, potentially paving the way for a new generation of autonomous soft robots. They also discovered that making individual components more active can paradoxically make the entire material less responsive, challenging a long-standing principle of engineering. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: Robert Macfarlane says trust in Cop to deliver change on climate is ‘misplaced’
item.description: Nature writer reveals in his first Reith lecture that he finds ‘much more hope’ in emerging alliances We are “misplacing our trust” in the Cop climate summits and their “capacity to deliver consequential change”, according to Robert Macfarlane in this year’s Reith lectures. In comments recorded before this week’s failure of the 31st UN climate summit to deliver an agreement on action to combat global heating , the bestselling author said he saw “much more hope” in emerging alliances such as the Santa Marta process , which is a smaller group of countries committed to phasing out fossil fuels… Publicado también por: The Guardian - Environment. Fuente: The Guardian - World.

item.title: Local measurements reveal global quantum properties in a constant number of experimental runs
item.description: A quantum device with more qubits is harder to verify. Describing a general quantum state takes an exponential number of parameters, and reconstructing it in full—a procedure known as state tomography—becomes impractical as the system grows. Yet most experiments do not need the full description. They need to know a few things: Is the state close to the target? Are the qubits entangled? And does the system carry the resources needed for quantum computation? Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Electron microscopy reveals the headquarters of poxviruses
item.description: Mpox remains a smoldering threat, with recent clusters in Brazil, Thailand and Austria and ongoing hot spots across multiple African countries. Other poxviruses also endanger human or animal health. A new study by the Institute of Science and Technology Austria (ISTA) uncovers the inner workings of the poxvirus core: how its gene-copying machines sit parked in dormant pairs, ready to print viral instructions and release them into the host cell through dedicated export portals embedded in the core shell. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Consumers, oblivious of being targeted, find online ads helpful
item.description: Most online shoppers know that ads strategically follow them across sites, a mechanism known as "ad retargeting." A new study led by Penn State researchers found that consumers find these targeted ads helpful, but explaining why they are seeing an ad can backfire by increasing concerns about being watched. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: NASA spacecraft data reveal how solar system's tail shifts over 14 years
item.description: A Southwest Research Institute-led study is the first to map out the distinct motion paths of the heliotail lobes across a 14-year period using data from NASA's Interstellar Boundary Explorer (IBEX) spacecraft. By identifying the paths followed by these lobes, the study provides a better understanding of how solar activity shapes the heliotail. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Physics-guided AI reconstructs fluid flow from sparse, noisy data
item.description: Medical imaging technologies have transformed how scientists and physicians visualize blood flowing through the human heart, but even the most advanced imaging techniques cannot capture every detail of fluid motion. Researchers at the University of California, Irvine, have developed a computational approach that combines fundamental physics with artificial intelligence to reconstruct a more complete and accurate picture of fluid flow from limited and imperfect measurements. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Overlooked symmetry group offers new geometric blueprint for the Standard Model and topologically protected vacuums
item.description: For more than half a century, physicists searching for a grand unified theory have followed one unspoken rule: go bigger. If you want to weave nature's fundamental forces into a single mathematical framework, the classic recipe says you need a giant "simple" symmetry group—structures like SU(5) or SO(10) that act like massive algebraic warehouses large enough to hold every force at once. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: A hidden link between a flower's color and its scent revealed
item.description: Researchers discovered that the biological machinery behind flower color also helps shape fragrance. By disrupting a single gene in petunias, they changed the flowers' mix of scent compounds, increasing some associated with vanilla and cloves. Fuente: Phys.org.
